The Post Boat , conveying the 1st February Mails, arrived here on Friday after a tedious passage from Barbados of 12 days, owing to the prevalence of calms and contrary winds. The papers are to the 2d of the month, and contain the þÿKing Speech s on the opening of Parliament, which took place on the 31st January. The new Session was opened by commission, and the Speech w as read by the Lord Chancellorþÿ it is as follows : þÿ þÿ Lords and Gentlemen , My We are commanded by his Majesty to acquaint you that his Majesty continues to receive from all Foreign Powers the strongest assurances of their friendly disposition, and his Majesty trusts that the experience of the blessings which peace confers upon nations tends to confirm and secure the present tranquility. þÿ His Majesty laments that the civil coniest which has agitated the Spanish Monarchy has not yet been brought to a close ; but his Majesty has continued to afford to the Queen of Spain that aid which, by the Treaty or Quadruple Alliance of 1834, his Majesty engaged to give, if it should become necessary : and his Majesty rejoices that his co-operating force has rendered useful assistance to tire troops of her Catholic Majesty. þÿ Events have happened in Portugal which for a time threatened to disturb the internal peace of that country, llis Majesty orderedt in consequence, a temporary augmentation of his naval force in the Tagus, for the more effectual protection of the persons and property of his subjects resident in Lisbon ; and the

His Majesty has directed them to be laid before you without delay. The increase of the revenue has hitherto more than justified the expectations created by the receipts of former years. His Majesty recommends an early renewal of your inquiries into the operation of the act permitting the establishment of Joint Stock Banks. The best security against mismanagement of banking

affairs must ever be lound in the capacity and integrity of those who are entrusted with the administration of them, and on the caution and prudence of the public. But no legislative regulation shall be omitted which can increase and ensure the stability of establishments upon which commercial credit so much depends. þÿ Lords and Gentlemen, My þÿ His Majesty has more especially come manded us to bring under your notice th. state of Ireland, and the wisdom of adopting all such measures as may improve the condition of that part of the United Kingdom. His Majesty commits these great interests into your hands in the confidence that you will be able to frame laws in accordance with the wishes of his Majesty and the expectations of his people. BORES OF MY ACQUANTANCE. Your professed story teller is a bore ; but your story teller who never finishes a story, is a bore ten times over. Tom endless never opens his lips but to tell you some anecdote or other, apropos of something or of nothing. You cannot name a person or allude to an event, or mention a place, but be recollects some curious incident, or interesting particular which are just brought to his mind, and which, while it is fresh in his memory, he really must relate. Tom, however, never related a whole anecdote in his life ; he resembles the late Marquis of Londonderry, whose parliamentrv speaking it has been said that he never concluded a sentence. Tom starts fair ; hut he seems to lose the scent immediately ; or other game coming in view, he cannot resist the temptation of following it, always letting the last object divert his attention from the former, until in the course of a þÿday hunt- s ing he has chased, perhaps twenty different foxes without taking a single brush. þÿ Mr. Endless, you carry a snuff-box, I believe ?" 1 could not have asked a more unlucky question. Never did I pay so dear for a pinch of snuff in my life. You shall hear. þÿ That snuff-box, sir, was my grandfather's ; he got it in a very odd way þÿ þÿI tell ll you the story. He had a favorite grey hound, which had been given to him by his friend Lord Broadland3 þÿ by the by, poor Lord Broadlands met a melancholy end ; he was travelling in Italy for the health of his daughter þÿ a celebrated beauty in her day t she

was married afterwards to a Col. Linstock, of the 15th Light Dragoons. A very curious circumstance occurred at the wedding. I have heard my father tell it a hundred times. J ust as the clergyman came to the words 4 honor and þÿobey, a Miss Clapperston þÿ I think her name was Clapperston observed some þÿ thing stirring under the Communion table, which she took for a mouse þÿ some ladies, you know cannot endure mice. My ow n mother met a serious accident once in consequence of a fright she got from a rat. Hats to be sure are odious creatures : but their cunning is wonderful. Lhd I never tell you what the rats did on board of the Tremendous, when my uncle had the command of her ? Well, þÿI tell ll it you now þÿ it will make you laugh. You remember my uncle? as gallant an officer as ever stepped upon quarter deck. He got his estate in Suffolk in a very singular manner þÿ you have heard me tell it? One day as he was walking in Piccadilly, an old gentleman, with a gold-headed cane in one hand, and a brown gingham umbrella in the other þÿ you may guess he was an oddity ; but old fellows are apt to be oddities ; there was my grandfather þÿhimself. Now, sir, seize your opportunity, and bring him back to the snuff-box ! þÿ Ay, ay, the snuff-box þÿ I am going to tell yon how my grandfather got it. Did you observe the miniature inside the lid ? It is the likeness of a Spanish lady who met with one of the strangest adventures you ever heard of A relation of my own met with an extraordinary adventure in Spain ; 1 had

better tell it to you while it is on my memory. The person I allude to was remarkably short of hearing. It is a great disadvantage to he short of þÿhearing. Disadvantage ! Its visitation in England was remarkable for its mildness, for its limitation to peculiar districts, and for its singularly capricious seizure of individuals. At Newcastle, while it lull heavily on one third of the town, the other two districts comparatively escaped. In London the seizures were chiefly in the narrower ports of the city, and the suburbs stretching along the river side. The only characteristic of the disease yet distinctly ascertainable is, that it exists with almost unfailing power in the vicinity of great rivers Beggary, squalidness, nakedness, and intoxication are all in danger ol attack. But damp and discomfort in the neighbourhood of great rivers appear to rendei its ravages almost inevitable. From the north of Germany it divided into two branches, one taking its course to England, and one sweeping to the south þÿ tr«l provinces of Germany suffered heavily, and Vienna lost a vast number of its poorer population. From Vienna, again, returning to the north, and crossing the Rhine, it entered France, passed through the provinces with comparatively slight mortality, but fell upon Pans vvitli redoubled venom. The mortality in iliat capital was unequaled ; within a few weeks twenty thousand died. The disease then seemed to pause. It suddenly started up in America, transferred none knew how. þÿ Alter ravaging the United States, it crossed the Lakes and the St. Lawrence, and spread terror through Canada. From Canada it made its way through the forests, and destroyed a

portion of the Indian population, which might have seemed to defy the inflictions of Europe in their unfathomable solitudes. But the cho. lera was not to be escaped, and the mortality was deeply fell among the thinned tribes of the vast countries stretching in the rear of the United States. Thence, by a sudden spring, it tell upon Mexico, tbc iiavanuali, and the Spanish settlements south of the line, finally wandering away into the deserts, until life .lesson, gradual went out, and disease could slay no more. þÿ It then crossed the Atlantic again, and threw Europe into new alarm at a disease which thus seemed to be marked for the perennial scourge of the earth. But its visitation, as it passed along, was now slight, until it reached the coniines of Mahometanism. There it swept all before it, as if kindled from some new furnace of wrath þÿ it devastated Egypt by thousands and tens of thousands. From Egypt it ascended to Constantinople There it rivalled the plague. Multitudes perished. It then partially returned to Russia and Germany. In the Polish War it fearfully increased the miseries of that time of wretchedness and blood Constantine the Archduke, closed his half insane and tyrannical life hy it ; and Dicbitsch, the famous passer of the Belkah, w ith a large share of the Russian army, were carried to the grave along with him. Spain, Portugal, and Italy still had escaped, and the world was asking by what means this singular preservation was effected, when the cholera broke out in Lisbon þÿ from Lisbon it pass-

ed to Madrid, and from Spain to Italy. In Jtiilv it is now raging. The cast coast has been seized within these few months, and Greece, the nearest shore, is tremblingly adopting measures of precaution. Bosnia, and the wild country bordering on the north of her kingdom, is already seized, and thousands are perishing day by day. When the science aud comforts of civilised countries have been so ineffectual, what resistance can he made hy the ignorance and wretchedness of barbarism. The disease will take its way

All have fallen, with more or less violence, upon the extremity of the continent, when it touched upon the realms ol Mahometanism þÿ always the original soil of the disease, and have thence gone regularly on, covering the earth with corpses, like the march of a destroying army. In the lesser plagues peculiar cities were ravaged, as in the plague of London, and like the þÿcen the violence of lever in a sick chamber, the disease terminated with the death of those seized within the limit, and beyond was harmless. But the cholera more resembled the floating of a cloud charged with elements of death þÿ here scarcely shadowing the atmosphere, there turning it into utter darkness þÿ in one region sweeping onward with uncontrolla. hie rapidity, in the next lingering till it almost ceased to move. Carried, as if by the chances of the wind, passing by kingdoms that lay directly in its path, hurrying to others across mountains and plains þÿ apparently omitting some whose poverty contained every predis-

position lbr disease, and fixing on others where every human power was ready to rep j its devastation, yet finally smitting all. It is not for us to weigh the wisdom of Providence, nor to announce its mysterious will. But if it had been that will to awake the mind of nations to a peculiar sense of a Supri me Being at tiiis time, or perhaps to prepare them for some moral and physical trial speedily demanding all their moral preparation, could at least the wisdom of man conceive a mote powerful teacher than the progress ol this strange and powerful agent ol mortality ? A yet unremitting, individual yet national, slow yet impressive, not destroying with one w ild burst of ruin, hut sparing even in the midst of destruction, and giving its teaching successively to every people of the civilized globe þÿ Can such things he, and he lor nothing ? Or does the declared course of Providence entitle us to believe that thc\ are? ORIGINAL ANECDOTES OF NATO LEON. In the table talk of Cambaceres, just published in Paris, there are three or four anecdotes of Napoleon, which we shall exit act. Here is one related by Count Fabre de I'Aude. þÿ It was his first interview with Bonaparte. " A man, designated under the name of P , and described by tbe count as a consummate scoundrel, one morning sought refuge in tbe count's apartment. At that moment (says the count) there was so violent a ringing at my door bell, that 1 was startled. þÿ P uttered a cry, which fortunately was smothered by his terror ; he then cast a wild look around him, leaped over my bed, and squatted down behind it. The door having been opened, a man was ushered in. Shall I describe him ? It is not possible. It was General Bonaparte Anger flashed from bis blue eyes, which had become dark with passion. Innocent as I was, I experienced the alarm of a guilty man. " I ain, I presume, at the residence of citizen Fabre dc l'Aude I" " You are citizen ; and I have the honor, I ' believe, of addressing General Bonaparte." þÿ You are right, and he comes peaceably, (peaceably indeed !) for information concern ing a scoundrel, a forger, and a calumniator. I will kill him, citizen of the Five hundred, if I can find him ; I will put him to death with my own hands." " May I ask the nature of his offence, General " On the one hand, he corresponds with the English Cabinet in my name; and, on tbe other, denounces me to the Directory as traitor to my country. þÿ What think of this, citizen Fabre I" " That,

with the sole exception of General Bonaparte' every one has a right to hang him. But you are a hero." " 1 am a man of honor, citizen' and am bound to punish a monster. I expect his address front you." " And from you," I replied, " 1 expect his pardon " I then pointed out to the General how he would debase himself by shedding the blood of so contemptable a wretch. After reflection for a few moments, he replied, " You are right I will spare his life. Undertake, however, to make liirn confess his baseness clearly, concisely, þÿ and without subterfuge. l.ct him appenr, from his own confession, as black as ink, and myself as white as snow. At this price he is safe, otherwise not." This ultimatum, uttered in a voice of thunder, was not to be resisted.
ATTS WUWA I promised all in the name of P : the General then said, " Citizen of the Five Hundred
I am delighted at having formed your acquaintance. Pray come and sec me. 1 have but little time I can call my own. I am to be married to-morrow, and must soon leave Paris."

Another anecdote is related by the Baron de Lamothe Langon himself. þÿ "One day when the sky was dark, the sun closely wrapped in thick vapours, and 1 was wandeiing through Paris, chance led me to the Louvre, At first I hesitated whether I should ascend to the picture gallery, or go through the halls of antiquities. My good star made me choose the latter, and this change from my original intention was not without influence over tbe remainder of my life. # # The Hunting Diana, that marvel of art, then placed in the room which Prudhon had decorated with so much talent, caught my attention. I stood pensive and motionless before this statue, and did not perceive that 1 was an ob. ject of curiosity to a person who had entered some time before, and was enjoying my enthusiasm. It was no less a personage than fiis Imperial Majesty He bad patiently waited during ten minutes, and patience was not one of his virtues; but finding that I remained absorbed in the contemplation of the Diana, he came close to me, and raising his hand, so as to engage my attention þÿ " Sir," said he, laughing, " do not forget that Pyg. malion fell in love with a statue " These words brought me back from the intellcctunj to this lower world, and I cast a glance towards the speaker, whom 1 knew to he the Emperor. Uncertain whether or not he wished to he known, I contented myself with bowing, ac. cording to the usage of the world, with regard to a superior. " Arc you a sculptor ?" " No þÿ Sir." Napoleon smiled at my marked lies

itation, which proved that I knew him. " A painter 1" " No, Sir," " What are you then V' said lie, somewhat impatiently. " 1 am a can. didate for those duties, in pursuing which a man may become useful to his sovereign " þÿ "You wish to be an Auditor in the State Gouncil ?" "Such is my desire!" "Who knows you ?" " Prince Cambac< res, and Count Fahre de I'Aude." " Your name ?" þÿ " I stated it " " Where is your father?" " j have lost him." " By emigration." " No he died on the scaffold in F5U4." " All ! yuU know me, and have only pretended that you did not." "You shall be a diplomatist." I ain the subject of your Imperial Majesty; was it my duty to raise the veil with which the Emperor was pleased to cover himself?-- " Well spoken ! very well ! Continue as you have begun, and you find the route easy which you have still to run. But above all things, he submissive."

St. Croix, CHRISTIA NSTE D, (MONDAY) June 26, 1837. Arrived in this Port this morning II. M's. Brig of War St. Thomas, Captain Graah, K. of I), after a passage of 45 days, on her anchoring Salutes were exchanged between her and Fort Christiansvaern.

The 2nd May packet from London bringing dates of the 15th, does not furnish many arti eles of great interest. The Lords have postponed the consideration of the Irish municipal bill until the 9th of June, this has caused great excitement in the house of Commons. Sir i' rancis Burdett has been again triumphantly returned as a member for Westminster, by a majority of 515. he was supported by the Consertative interest, and his re-election indicates a re- action in public opinion. (From the Barbadian, June 10.) France. þÿ We have received the Paris papers of Thursday, by which we learn that the Charte of Wednesday night contained the fob lowing paragraph, which seems to have given nearly universal satisfaction in Paris The King has designed to commute the punishment of death awarded against Meunier to transportation. The President of the Court of Peers went himself to announce this intelligence to Meunier, who testified the liveliest sentiments of repentance and gratitude. "We have been so fortunate," savs the Journal des Debuts, as to become acquitted with some of the circumstances which have attended the spontaneous act of royal clemen-

cy towards Meunier, and we have great pleasure in communicating them to the public, be. cause they display in all his simple and Majestic grandeur the King whom France has raised to the throne of July, and whom base calumny still assails, even in that inviolable sphere in which the respect of the people has placed him. Meunier, immediately alter his sentence was pronounced, wrote to the King, humbly intreating pardon, in terms of the most sincere repentance. But before his petition reached his Majesty, the council of ministers was considering this serious question ; and the King himself had spoken in favour of commutation, considering the good sentiments the culprit several times expressed during the proceeding þÿ in fact, the ordonance was signed before Meunier's petition was brought to the council. At the same moment an aged woman entered the court of the p&lace, scarcely able to walk from her extreme distress of mind. She urgently entreated to be allowed to deliver a petition to the Queen. 'Twas the unhappy mother of Meunier. The officers of the palace received her with kindness, and immediately went to receive the Queen's orders. In a few minutes afterwards the supplicant was on her knees at the feet of her Majesty, battling her royal hands with tears, and praying for mercy with convulsive sobs. The Queen was yet uninformed of the decision of the council, and would onlv return consolatory language, trembling at the idea of giving false hopes. During this affecting

scene the door opened, the King was announced, and lrom his own mouth put an end to the perplexities of the Queen by informing the mother of the regicide that the life of her son was spared. ' I have commuted his punishment, said his Majesty. ' Your son has repented, and 1 have wished him to live. I did not wait for his petition to pronounce his pardon.' As the unfortunate woman was completely embarrassed and overcome at finding herself in the presence of so much goodness as well as grandeur, and could only replv to it with her tears, the King added ; Be comforted ! V our son is already acquainted with his pai don. 1 have just sent the President of the Court of Peers to make it known to him.' J he King then raised the poor woman, who still remained on her knees at the Queen's feet, and seated her in an arm-chair, continuing to uddiess her in terms of consolation and benevolence. After a few minutes more their Majesties retired, recommending Madame Meunier, still oppressed with her emotions, to the care of their officers.

A New Claimant to tiie Throne, þÿ At the sitting of' the King's Bench, Dublin, on Wednesday, a respectable looking man, dressed in black, and whose appearance denoted anything but insanity, addressed the Lord Chief Justice thus " Mv lord, I appear before your lordship under circumstances of no ordinary description þÿ circumstances which may at a future period involve this great empire in unexampled diificultics. My Lord, it is not perhaps generally known that a son was born to his late most gracious Majesty George the Fourth, in the year 1797, by an illustrious princess, Queen Caroline ot Brunswick ; and that, influenced by the destinies which await us all, that son came over to Ireland at a very early age, and took up his residence in Kerry. From that period he has been lost sight of by bis family-; and as ano. ther illustrious personage is now deemed heir presumptive to the throne of these kingdoms, 1 feel it my duty to warn you, my loid, as his Majesty's representative in this Court, and from this spot to warn all other judges, magistrates, and all his Majesty's liege subjects throughout these realms, lest they should be guilty of misprision of treason, that 1 am that son, and therefore lawlul heir to the crown- I have appealed to the House of Lords, and to the other members of the royal family, who have univerally acknowledged me to be the unhappy and long lost child of the illustrious prince now no more. My Lord, my name is the Lev. llobert M'Giilicuddy." During the

delivery of this extraordinary address, the Lord Chief Justice listened with the most polite attention, while the bar at intervals were convulsed with laughter. This most singular individual then bowed gracefully to the Court and the bar, and immediately left the court. þÿ Dublin paper.

We have heard with considerable satisfaction of a few circumstances connected with Military affairs in these Colonies, which reflect great credit on the Government, but more especially on that distinguished Officer, | Lord Hill, from whom, we have no doubt, the improvements in contemplation have emanated. We learn that the Garrison of Saint Ann's is to be considerably strengthened ; that four Regiments are to be constantly stationed here, all of them European Regiments ; the 1st West India Regiment, composed of Blacks, to be largely increased, and confined chiefly to the other Colonies. That, in future, the Regiments for this Command, instead of being sent direct from England or Ireland to this climate, will serve for a certain period in the Mediterranean (Malta, we suppose), from I thence be removed to the West Indies, and after three years service in these Colonies (not longer), proceed to Canada. This regulation will greatly promote the health of the troops þÿ the Mediterranean being a warm, though temperate climate, the soldiers will be not so liable to West India fevers on being removed from thence, as they were when transported suddenly from England. We are informed that three new Barracks are to be built at Saint Ann's; and þÿ what has long been a great desideratum þÿ a Chapel. This will be an important acquisition to the troops, and to the families of the Officers in Garrison, and, we may add, a comfort to the Chaplain. A steamer is expected soon from England,

which will be placed at the entire disposal of His Excellency the Commander of the Forces. This will greatly facilitate the conveyance of troops and stores from one Colony to another. We rejoice to hear that the comforts ol the soldier are now greatly increased. The men arc served now, we understand, with fresh beef5 days in the week þÿ a change materially important to their health þÿ and other allowances, we hear, are increased.

It is among the old maxims that the understanding is always the dupe of the heart. 1 am afraid that there is not so much error of this kind in the world as there used to bo. I j is indeed what he do not mean that the understanding of mankind rn general lias become too elevated to be so easily duped as it used to be, but 1 do mean that there is for the most part no heart to dupe it. Indulgence is now an affair of calculation, not an error arising from the absence of calculation. The understanding, instead of being duped unto error by sentiment, rebels against right, and takes the wrong way upon deliberation. It is quite unfashionable to have a heart, even as an excuse for the mistakes of the head.

The man of integrity is one who makes it his constant rule to follow the road of Duty, according as the word of God, and the voice of his conscience, point it out to him. He is not guided merely by affections, which may sometimes give the color of virtue to a loose and unstable character. The upright man is guided by a fixed principle of mind, which determines him to esteem nothing but what is honouiable, and to abhor whatever is base or unworthy, in moral conduct. Hence we find him ever the same at all times: the trusty friend, the affectionate relation, the conscientious man of business, the pious worshiper, the public-spirited citizen, lie assumes no borrowed appearance. He seeks no mask to cover liiin, for lie acts no stupid part ; but he appears to be þÿ full of truth, candour, and humanity. In all his pursuits, he knows no path but the fair and direct one ; and would much rather fail of success than attain it by reproachful-means. He never shows us a smiling countenance while lie meditates evil against us in his heart. He never praises us among our friends and then joins introducing us among our enemies. We shall never find one part of his character at variance with another. In his manners he is simple and unaffected : in all his proceedings, open and consistent.

XACTSX. MONEY. MARKET a-.d CITY INTELLIGENCE- Saturday Evening, April 29.

To those who are watching the progress of the great American experiment for establishing a paper circulation in this country, the announcement will not be read with iudifierence, that bills to the amount of 1,000,000/. have been shipped by the packet which has just arrived, and which sailed on the 10th instant. This occurred also, which is very material to be observed, when it was not known what reception they were likely to experience here, and when doubts existed, as some of the letters state, whether they would find currency at all. Those who believe, then, that the United States Bank and other banks and joint-stock companies in New- York will voluntarily desist from sending when they find such markets open, and so effectual a relief provided for difficulties at home, must have minds provided with reasoning powers of a very peculiar kind. The crisis in New York, at the date of these accounts, among the trading interest, had reached a degree of intensity to which none of the previous accounts furnish any parallel. In the statements of failures they are so alarming, and describe the calamity to be of so sweeping and general a nature, as almost to outrage belief Before adopting them implicitly, it seems prudent to wait for further intelligence, but it may be mentioned that one of the private letters, the credibility of which there is no reason to doubt, states that there had occurred near a hundred failures in New York alone, and estimates the total amount of them at not

less than 3,000,000/. The classes upon whom the mischief has fallen are then enumerated in order ; but, without any close knowledge of the internal state of that city, it may be inferred that the major part of these must be speculators and persons of no note, whose fall can exercise no influence beyond its limits þÿ Such was the determination of the banks, whatever assistance they might give in paper, not to allow themselves to be run upon for gold, that notices had been given in some instances, and where it had not the fact was well understood, that where customers proposed taking specie they would be requested to withdraw their accounts. The premium on specie, whether gold or silver, was from 1 to 1| per cent. The news from England, when it shall bo received, that the bills and bonds have got into ready circulation here, will be among the most welcome, probably, that has ever reached the trading community of New York. To the casualties under which our commerce with America is suffering has been added one in another department of our trade þÿ that with the East Indies, which is little inferior to it in importance. We refer to the stoppage of the eminent house of Marjoribanks and Ferrers, which has taken place today, and has added much to the distrust about private credit which before prevailed, especially as this is the second great house in that line which has stopped during the week. been uttered þÿ (says the Ncw-YorkGazctte) no foresight, however keen, was able to penetrate the veil which is now withdrawn from the political and commercial horizon. For many months it has been apparent to those who best understood mercantile affairs, that our immense indebtedness to European countries, our deranyed state of currency, combined with other causes, must result in a catastrophe little expected by the great body of the community. But the curtain is raised before the actors are dressed, the orchestra in tune, or the theatre occupied. Let us call to mind recent events. was unusually depressed þÿ During the past winter the the money market best paper was refused discount at the banks, was thrown into the market as an article of merchandize, and sold at a rate which threatened ruin to the drawer. A portion of our merchants weathered the gale, while others were thrown on the coast. The commercial history of nations probably does not furnish a parallel to that ol our own at the present time A cloud which arose no bigger than a man's hand, while most of os were reposing in fancied security, has overwhelmed the land, and with the destructive effects of a tornado carried desolation in its course. All leel its influence, however remote from the immediate scene of desolation. It is less than ten weeks since the intelligence of a great commercial failure came with the effect of a thunderbolt from the south. Simultaneously with this news, and as if ominous of ulterior events, fell to the ground

an edifice which had scarcely been completed, in this city, in which it was contemplated to centre vast financial operations. In three days afterward, its projectors, extensively engaged in business, declared themselves bankrupt. In their train fell many firms, some of long standing, and enjoying unlimited confidence at home and abroad. Others followed to an alarming extent, till several hundred houses, employing a capital of a hundred millions, are prostrated in the general ruin. Nor is this destruction confined to New York. Each successive mail has brought with it intelligence of heavy failures in all the cities on the Atlantic coast The contagion has flown with the wings of an eagle, and its operation resembles that of a commercial cholera. These disasters are not limited to individuals, but all our public institutions are in consequence vitally affected. Factories are aban doned, the shops of artizans closed, building suspended, and thousands of workmen thrown out of employment. Our banks in all parts of the continent have suspended payments in specie ; a paper currency is the only one which is afloat, and the effect is, that the National Government is an acknowledged defaulter. Even the very-gold which was received in part payment of the French indemnity is withheld from its rightful owners, and the paper of insolvent banks tendered in its stead. In addition to this catalogue of evils which are pressing upon us like an incubus, our mer cantile drafts have been returned dishonored

from abroad, even before our transatlantic friends were aware of the storm that had encompassed us. Doubts, fears and anxieties still exist for the future ; and many, w ho yet remain apparently firm, are reminded by every wind that blows of the admonition þÿ "let hint that thinketh he standeth, take heed lest he fall." As it must necessarily be a great length of time before business will resume its wonted course, even should the ensuing session of Congress adopt the most judicious measures to attain that event, we shall have profited little, if in the interim our course has been marked by extravagance, negligence or idleness ; and when it shall please Providence to said that " the rain descended and the floods restore us again to prosperity, let it not be came, and the winds blew and beat upon that house and it fell, for it was built upon the, sand."
A mercantile friend at New York writes us, under date of Tuesday, as follows : " Business of all sorts þÿ is most horribly dull iu this city. The season

" of the cholera, in '32, bore nocomuarison w ith this spring. Our streets in the business part of the day resemble the Sundays of ordinary times The merchants stand at their doors with folded arms, while thousands of clerks have been thrown out of employment, and are wandering about upon the " sea of uncertainty." or have returned to their country homes, those who are so fortunate as to have any Our public houses, which at this time of year, are generally crowded, present now a most " beggarly account of empty" beds. The result of the mad measures of the administration, presents its blighted aspect at every turn, and the heart sickens at the contemplation thereof. From the multitudes out of employment here, it would appear next to impossible to escape rebellion unless speedy reliel be afforded them."

Our Demerara papers received on Wednesday last, touch but very lightly upon the subject of the malignant epidemic prevailing in Georgetown ; but the obituaries they contain, present ample proofs of its fatal and melancholy ravages. We cannot but sympathise deeply with our fellow colonists upon

this afflicting visitation, well knowing by our situation last year, when that scourge, yellow fever, prevailed here, what theirs must be, under similar circumstances, and sincerely hope it may please the allwise disposer of events shortly to restore health to the Colony.

According to accounts contained in the journals ot those islands visited by small pox, we are glad to learn, it is on the decline in most of them, and has nearly disappeared from others. The painful truth that the morwhich it has occasioned has been great, cannot however be concealed. In Grenada, Irinidad, and Saint Christopher, its eflects have been more severely felt; in the last mentioned island nearly 1500 persons were attacked in one parish, of which over 50 have died ; the other two islands have been no less sufferers by it. As yet, we have been quite free from it, owing to the punctual and right enforcement of the quarantine law, which is still in force. þÿ Ibid. Mail Boat this morning from British oo rf,£r!:t t0 bear by the arrival of the Guiana, that fever was still prevailing most fatally in Demerara. Many deaths are reported iii the papers. þÿ I he Barbadian July 5.

The only intelligence of import received by vessels which have arrived here since the Mail-boat, is that of the alarming prevalency of what is described as Yellow Fever in De merara. So calamitous has been its progress, that, by a private letter received, we learn that in a very short period no less than upwards of 35 deaths ensued from Fever, in one street þÿ Most of the stores, (says the writer ot another letter) seem deserted by tbeir þÿClerks. The progress of this visitation seems to be paralysing trade ; whilst whether it be actually Yellow Fever, in which the apprehensions ot the people pre-dispose them for the contagion, or an epidemic of a different character, the mortality seems on the increase to an appalling amount. The suddenness with which this intelligence has come upon us, (per the Hebe) naturally found us unprepared with the proper precautionary measures of a Fever quarantine. And this circumstance induces an additional reflection on the extreme negligence attending the transmission of the Island papers, as alluded to in our last Paper and promiscuously by the Island Journals in general. It is alone by such a medium of information þÿ viz the certified Medical Reports of the state of health of the various Colonies, and the precautionary measures of the authorities respecting them, þÿ that we can be forewarned. VVc mentioned in last week's Paper, that we had received no Guiana papers for three Mad-boats preceding ; and it followed, as may be inferred, that it was only to
such a chance communication as that of the Hebe , we could have been enabled to guard ourselves against the reputed cotagion. þÿ The Barbadian July 5.

The American Packet-Ship Wellington. þÿ Through the kindness of Captain I). Chadwick, her commander, we were on Thursday favoured with a sight of this vessel, which is In every way worthy of her name. The Wellington performed he maiden voyage from New York in the short space of JO days, which was at least a week sooner than any other ship leaving for England at the same period ; but, from the beautiful symmetry of her form, no one could have doubted her capabilities as a sailer. The frigate-like modelling of her bows appears to us to be especially worthy the attention of the connoisseur in naval architecture. As regards the inte rior, the fittings and arrangements for the accommodation of passengers are as elegant and complete as can be possibly imagined. The American ships are celebrated for their magnificence, but the Wellington surpasses all we have ever seen. The cabins are lofty and so sumptiously decorated that her passengers might fancy themselves in the apartments of a nobleman. The furniture is of the costliest kind ; the joinery rich and tasteful, the workman having called to his aid materials of the most superior description Satin, rose, and zebra wood, and the fine black American walnut, are made to contribute their varied beauties. Captain Chadwick informs us that, conceiving his new ship to be in all respects the finest that ever was built, his owners at New York were desirious that she should receive a name ot a corresponding order. That of

þÿ the first captain of the age" was accordingly thought ol and adopted, and a well executed bust of the illustrious warrior graces the bow of the vessel. The Wellington will leave the St Katharine Docks in þÿ f a ew days, for New York, full of goods and passengers. þÿ W e wish her success, þÿ London Taper.

Uses of Biography. Counsels, like compliments, are best conveyed in an indirect and oblique manner ; and this renders biography as well as fable a most convenient vehicle for instruction. An ingc- | nious gentleman was asked what was the best lesson for youth ; he answered, The life ol a good man. Being again asked what w as the next best, he replied, The a life of a bad one. þÿ ! The first would make him in love with virtue, and teach him how to conduct himself through life, so as to become an ornament to society and a blessing to his family and friends ; and the last would point out the hateful and horrid consequences of vice, and make him careful to avoid those actions which appeared so detestable in others. þÿ Goldsmith.

LORD BEXLEY, the President, on taking the Chair, addressed the Meeting as follows: þÿ My Lords, Ladies, and Gentlemen ! þÿ I have again the honour to welcome you to the Anniversary of the British and Foreign Bible Society ; and while I aoknow ledge, with humble gratitude, that Providence which for so many successive years has enabled me to assume this chair, either as the representative of your late lamented President, 01 in the station in which vour partial kindness placed me at his decease, 1 have the pleasure of seeing, in the appearance of the Hall, unequivocal proofs of the undiminished interest taken by the British Public in the cans'- of the Bible Society ; and, what is far more important, in the cause of the Bible itself. For when I observe, year after year, this spacious Hall not less completely filled than the smaller room which we formerly occupied on such occasions, and find that the recurrence of successive Meetings seems to abate nothing of the prevailing anxiety to attend them, I feel great satisfaction in the conviction, that this anxiety is to be attributed, not so much to the influence of mere curiosity, or to the gratification experienced in listening to »he exertions of oratorical talent, as to a steady and |>ersevering zeal for the triumph of Truth, and for the establishment of our þÿRedeemer kingdom s upon earth The review of the Proceedings of the Society, as described in the Report of the Committee, will afford many subjects of congratu-

lation, both as respects the extent of its opera' tions and the amount of it., resources: and it is a no less plea ;:p subject ol reflection, that while the world at large is torn by many elements of discord, from which our own country has by no means been exempted, tbe internal aspect ol the British and Foreign Bible Society lias been peaceable and tranquil. þÿ The course of the year now closed has not indeed been one of unmingled pleasure. It has been marked by public grief and pr-'-ate sorrow. Some of our early and venerable þÿpatrons some of our most steady and liberal þÿfriends and almost the last of the original Olficcrs of the Society, who nursed it in its infancy, have been taken from us. The first generation of the Bible Society nearly pass- is ed away: þÿ but you will remember, that the work of the Bible Society is not (unless we could hope for miraculous interposition and assistance) the work of one generation. To publish the Scriptures in every language of the world þÿ to diffuse them among all the nations ot the earth þÿ and, as we have been commanded by our Lord, to preach the Gospel to every þÿcreature is not, without supernatural aid, within the compass of the life of man þÿ V ot let us be thankful for what, by the Divine Blessing, It as been done. We have laid the þÿteousness alone truly þÿ oundution deep and wide, by such a multiplication ol Versions of the Scriptures as the woild has never before seen : we have opened communications with almost every coast,
and scattered the seed þÿ thinly indeed, but þÿWidely throughout every continent; foreign

Mv Lord, numerous as have been t fie topics touched upon in the Report just j read, there is one which w\as briefly glanced j at, both in the commencement and in the conclusion of it, upon which 1 may perhaps be allowed to say a few words Whatever may have been the anxieties and alarms arising from passing events, with respect to the future prospects of this Society, 1 do humbly conceive that the present Meeting is both an answer and an antidote to those alarms. LORD G LENT, LG. þÿ My Lord, Ladies, and Gentlemen. The reluctance with which, notwithstanding the interest I feel in this Institution, I must always present myself to you, is increased on this occasion, because I am summoned to act as the substitute of a Right Rev. Prelate, whose oilier most important avocations have compelled him to relinquish the þÿtask -the pleasing task, as, he assured me, he felt it to he þÿ of proposing to von this Resolution. Entreating, therefore, your indulgence, I rise, in the absence of the Bishop of Chichester, to propose to you a Resolution, generally expressive of your satisfaction at the progress of the Society, and your anxious solicitude for its future success ; and exhorting all its friends to ardour in this great cause. Happily for me, the Motion is one which requires but little eloquence in its support ; and the cause is one which is above all human eloquence. Happily for me, I am not called upon to stimulate those who are unwilling, or to rouse those who are slumbering; hut to join with you in expressing your feelings as well as mine þÿ the feelings of gratitude and congratulation. But I confess that I rise on tins occasion, as I have on others of the same

tmcs. Mi0rJk.a&md kind, with no small degree of misgiving ; because I see around me those who, by personal exertions and personal services, during the intervals of its Annual Meetings, have advanced this cause. It seems, therefore, somewhat presumptuous in one to rise who had no personal sacrifices to make, and who has made no personal exertions ; whom, in fact, other avocations and duties have precluded from those personal efforts, which are, I conceive, the bust recommendation to your favour I see around me those who, coming from distant lands, are prepared to communicate to you the result, of their labours: and I think your time is almost misspent, if I intervene to delay the gratification you may expect from their reports But l am consoled by thinking, that the object of these Meetings is not merely t receive communications from those who are personally engaged, hut also that those who are prevented from personal interposition mat have an opportunity of assuring you of their unabated sympathy with you, and declaring their continued allegiance to this sacred cause. These Annual Meetings are, indeed, formed to collect and gather together the results of the periods that elapse between their succession. In the twelve months that have passed since the last Meeting, we have heard from different parts of t he world þÿ from the East, the West, the North,' and the South þÿ for we embrace all quarters of the globe in our various ramifications : we have had communications from different So-

cieties and Local Associations, who have forwarded, in succession, an account of their efforts. As in an extensive battle-field, along a wide frontier, various hands are aiming at the same object, but separated from each other as mountains rise and forests intervene, vet ever and anon is heard from afar the sound of conquest, the cheering cry of battle, and the glorious shouts of victory : so too, in these Annual Meetings, while during the interval, we Inve heard thfs sound from different parts of the globe, here we muster and concentrate our gathered energies: here our various hands unite and are welcomed : and the echo of gratulation is hurled hack, through a thousand channels, to the remotest quarters of the globe. It is, indeed, highly satisfactory to perceive, that this Institution þÿ and this is no slight praise keeps pace with the activity and en- þÿ ergy of the age. My Lord, the motto of this age is, þÿVelocity. Throughout the whole þÿ sphere of society, in all science and art, in physical and mental exertion, there is a rush and tempest of effort, which has never before been exhibited And might vve not, then, have expected, that, possibly, those institutions which rely on more ethereal elements might iiave failed to participate in the vulgar excitement ? But no ! the spirit that animates this Institution can compare with the noblest efforts of any other motives ! I find, that, during the last year, this Society has realized greater resources than on any former occasion ; and I

think I see in this Meeting that determination, which enables me to prophesy, that, in succeeding years, you will have to offer the same congratulations. To those who are in the habit of associating mighty exertions of mind with tlm efforts of angry passions and animosity, it is a state of no common interest or common refreshment to perceive the developemcnt of great mental and physical power, unsophisticated and unpolluted by any defilement þÿ It is something, to stop from the tumults and

My Lord, it gave me the highest satisfaction to hear, both from the Report and in the speech of the Right Reverend Prelate who h.is just sat down, deductions from the nature of this Institution, such as must have delighted this Assembly : and still more delightful was it to hear them from the lips ol one of the distinguished ornaments of onr Established Church. If, indeed, the Cross be j Wolffs Hoc. our standard, then, not only in those few mo. ir ents in which we arc assembled here, should

we lay aside all angry passions and discordant interests of common life, but, at all times, we who are engaged in this cause ought to he distinguished by that spirit of benevolence, which is its fundamental principle, and its chief and primary object. Why is it that Christendom (and this Society embraces all Christendom,) furnishes so j many examples of the followers of Him whose i essence was Charity, yet destroying themselves and each other þÿ entering into minute I and non-essential quarrels? þÿ w hy, but because ( their contemplation is not intent on that banner which they profess to follow ? My Lord, it' on that memorable occasion, when that standard was first elevated, amid the ignominy and taunts of a murderous multitude þÿ if, when it first bore its innocent and spotless and Divine Victim, to the shame and derision of men, and amid the confusion and convulsion of sympathizing nature þÿ if, at that overwhelming moment, the followers of that crucified Master had been found disputing at the very foot of the Cross on matters of trivial import þÿ if it had been, not the soldiers, but the Disciples, who were parting his garments by lot þÿ what should we have thought of that desperate ingratitude and atrocity ? But arc not these circumstances immortal ; and is not this event perpetual ? and is not the spectacle before our eyes? Have we not seen the shame, and witnessed all the calamities consequent on that scene ? þÿ and yet, while we profess to follow that banner, we þÿ waste our
time in useless altercations ! þÿ I do trust that the effect of this Meeting will he, to produce a greater extent of those feelings of charity which have been so warmly and eloquently inculcated.

VVe wore again favoured with several re freshing showers last week, and on Saturday morning from about daydawn almost as much rain fell as we had on the 30th ultimo The soil acknowledges the bounty of heaven by putting on its gay mantle of green, and given every promise of plenty. We sincerely congratulate not only the planters, but the inhabitants of every part of the Island, for it is only when the earth yields her fruits to the Agriculturist that all thrive. The execution of the man Robert, whose conviction and sentence of death, for the attempted murder of his master, Mr. Gim., we have already noticed, took place on Monday last, amidst an immense concourse of persons. The awful and melancholy scene was rendered more distressing by the breaking of a first, and second rope used in the execution of the wretched culprit. A third rope doubled, as we understand, at last terminated his sufferings. We saw nothing of the dismal procession, nor of the execution ; but we are informed that the Chaplain of the Gaol, and Mr. Joseph Thorne, attended the criminal ; and we hear that in the course of their visits to him, they failed in obtaining from him any confession of his guilt. To the last moment of his existence, we learn that he protested Ins innocence. þÿ Ibid,

An Electrical þÿChild.- -A young lady of Lille was lately put to bed with a child which gave a sort of electrical shock to the surgeon who brought it into the world. MAY 31, 1837. THE RIGHT HON. LOUD BEXLEY IN THE CHAIR. EARL OF þÿHARROWBY. Ladies and Gentlemen, Having had the honour of being called upon by the Noble President to second the motion of the Noble Lord who lias just sat down, I feel unwilling not to respond to that call. I am, however, in a state both of health and voice, that makes it impossible for me to address more than a very few words to you, in this great Assembly : þÿ but even under all these disadvantages, having been called upon, 1 am not willing to lose this opportunity of testifying my unabated allegiance, and, I trust, increased admiration of this Society. And although 1 have not to comfort myself with the recollection of having been one of those who have made any exertions towards furthering this great cause and am, there- þÿ fore, in one respect in a similar position with my noble friend who has just sat down þÿ yet I consider it, and have always considered it, a great privilege to be able occasionally to express the sentiments which 1 have now stated ; and, at a time of life when the opportunity of doing so many perhaps never again be afforded me, I am unwilling to let this day pass, without having renewed that expression. I need not attempt to repeat what has been stated to you with so much force and eloquence by the Noble Lord þÿ the peculiar satisfaction that we feel, in these times of excitement on many other subjects of inferior moment, however important they may be in themselves, that the spirit of the public mind has been directed with increased vigour to-

wards the furtherance of the great object for which we are here assembled þÿ I find that it wonld be impossible for me to proceed further; and therefore conclude, in a humble discharge of what 1 conceive to be a most sacred duty, by seconding the motion.

Rev. Dr. Cox, of Hackney. þÿ My Lord, Among other considerations which encourage us in the support of the important Institutions whose Anniversaries we meet to commemorate, is this ; þÿ great Societies not only unite all parties, but improve all : they have a tendency to purify our motives, to inspirit our zeal, and to rub off our asperities. While, therefore, there is a direct benefit to the world in the distribution of the Holy Scriptures there is this incidental and indirect benefit to ourselves ; and thus the Bible, which we propose to circulate, moves on with a train of blessings. If there were no good actually done by the direct distribution of the Scriptures ; and if there were not that amount of good accomplished which we believe there is, and of which we have intelligence every day ; it there were not those numerous sick beds, and dying beds, which the Bible is calculated to console, and which it is every day consoling: if all those great results did not occur at the various and distant parts of the earth, which we know do occur ; still our combining together, in one effort, is both elevating and ennobling. .When we contemplate a little object, the mind contracts ; and in proportion

JDAW3JR T33V3Sri>a31£ 3s203'Ji:B31TT>3 AT33. as we rise to the contemplation and advocacy of great objects, the mind expands. There is, in our moral constitution, a tendency to itself to the object which is presented before our view : and on this ground I rejoice in the Bible Society. My Lord, when we touch and circulate the Bible, we touch immortality ; we raise the minds of individuals and of nations to contemplate the fact that they are immortal ; we show them the path to immortality ; and we grasp an object, which, by this natural re-action and influence on ourselves, raises us to a higher and still higher degree of moral elevation. 1 know, My Lord, there was a period, and not a very distant one þÿ a period, in fact, within the recollection of multitudes now before me, when, in the boasted predictions of Infidelity, it was declared, that there should be no Bible Society ; there were to be no Associations formed for the extension of Christianity ; Christianity itself, with all its institutions, was to be no more ; þÿ and in those predictions, the very period at which we have arrived was the period in which, according to them, the ploughshare of destruction w as to pass over Christendom, and all the institutions of our Christian country. Yet, w hat is the tact ? At this very moment this Society is marching, with the Bible in its hand, over the graves of its denoucers, and of the denouncers of Christianity, to that universal dominion, which I trust it will obtain, over the minds of all mankind, and through all gene-

rations of time ! There are many considerations to encourage us. Consider, for a moment, the sublimity of the position in which we are placed. þÿ Philosophical speculation, or þÿ þÿdiscovery if you please, has represented that there is a gravitating centre, which is the central point of all the movements, concurrent and contradictory, that appear in the visible heavens, and which are extended through the invisible regions space of in the universe ; and 1 have sometimes thought what a sublime point it would be to occupy, could some intelligent being stand there, capable of looking through the vast machinery around him, analyzing the movements of those mighty orbs through all their revolutions, and seeing this great influence combining and preserving all in their places But, My Lord, ! what is fancy in one case, is fact in another. We are placed, at this moment, with the Bible in our hands, in that central point of light and influence ; þÿ we are standing at that point in the moral universe, from which we can look abroad, and see the ten thousand various movements of the moral world combined and united, and made to concur, under the sustaining power and government of God, by that Power which is influencing and directing all : þÿ and I, for one, would say, Perish all those sentiments and feelings that are not in concurrence with the great object of this Society ! a Society, which is standing in this great point of glorious light and energy, holding all that is apparently contradictory in its movements in one

great bond of brotherhood and association ; being not only the point of gravity, but the central light of the moral world ; diffusing, on systems and Associations, light and influence þÿ itself the centre, and they revolving round it ! 1 would w ish, for one, ever to stand in this central point, and look around with gratitude to God for what has been accomplished, with a for.d remembrance of departed 'saints who, from an early period, have adorned this Society, and advanced its interests ; and with

joyful anticipation of that moment, when, through the all-controling ndght oi ihat principle to which I have referred, þÿ Denominations of Christians all people þÿ all Christen- all dom þÿ all lands þÿ all worlds, shall unite in the great, harmonious, and heavenly strain, Hal- þÿ leluiah 1 for the Lord God Omnipotent reigneth þÿ1

Rev H. RA1KES, Chancellor of the Diocese of Chester. þÿ My Lord, Ladies and Gentlemen, I rejoice that the Resolution 1 hold in my hand is one which w ill require little from the individual who addresses you at present, and nothing to recommend it to your acceptance : þÿ it is, That the thanks of this Meeting be given to our Noble President, and to the Vice-Presidents, for their continued patronage and support. But let me state the ground on which I feel that the present situation of the Society is a subject of congratulation. It is not only gratifying to hear of the enlargement of its funds, and of the extension of Christianity throughout the world ; it is not merely a blessed thing to follow the distribution of Bibles through regions which seemed to have been hermetically sealed against the Gospel ; it is not merely a blessed thing to hear of the eagerness and gratitude of the people who reside in distant China, and of those vast kingdoms of the East and West which have so long seemed impervious to the influence of the Scriptures; but there are other subjects <>f congratulation, which for themselves at present on my feelings. I rejoice in the enlargement of the funds of this Society, not merely on account of the good effect produced without, but for the testimony it affords also of the state within. It carries to my mind a firm, distinct conviction, that the great spring of Religion is sound and firm among us ; and that, whatever may be the dangers without þÿ

whatever may excite apprehension or alarm there þÿ there is a sound and healthy temperament within. And this, too, has often strpek me, that as the pulse is to the body of n man, so is the Bible Society to the work of Religion at large. Whatever may be the disease of the body, still we know, that if the pulse beats sound and true, the physician bids his patient to take good courage. So I trust that the report of the state of funds of the British and Foreign Bible Society proves that the health of our Religion is not in danger. þÿ But there are other circumstances not to be lost sight of: þÿ for the condition of our Society proves, not only that the spring of Religion is sound within, but that the pure Protestant feeling is still alive. It proves, that, whatever may be our doubts and misgivings, there is a sound feeling of veneration for the word of God, and a disposition bring every opinion to that to standard, and to revert to the law and the Testimony as the only standard of all truth. In times like the present, I feel that this circumstance is not without its weight. I have, no doubt, my feelings as a Churchman þÿ have what may be called my prejudices ns a Churchman : but this 1 can safely say ; I can anticipate no event in the religious world which would carry such pain to my heart, or fill me with such deep sadness, as any appearance of a falling-oil in the resources of the British mid Foreign Bible Society, or of a shaking of that union in w hich so many are joined to promote the distribution of
the Scriptures of þÿtruth. But, beyond tin's, it is encouraging to observe, that the spirit of Christian charity and love is not running cold among us. I acknowledge that 1 had my

fears, I had my doubts, as to what would be the tenor of the Report this day. But 1 rejoice that these doubts and fears are dispelled ; that the golden chain which links the different members of the body of Christ together is not weakened: that the noble purpose which aims to include all the kingdoms of the earth in one kingdom is not shaken. Whatever may be the apparent difference of opinion amongst us, there is still a sound practical feeling of love to God and good-will towards men. If therefore, we see Christian love struggling against the convulsions of the moment, and that it is not subdued by these convulsions, then, I trust, we may believe, that, as the wind which shakes the oak of our country only strengthens and increases the nourishment it derives from its roots, so all disputes and agitations without will only strengthen the great work of Religion in our hearts, and give a lovelier influence to that blessed Gospel of our Lord and Saviour, which it is our privilege to distribute.

LORD þÿBEXLEY. Ladies and Gentlemen, In the name of my coadjutors and myself, beg I leave to tender you our thanks. I am happy to see so large a number of Vice Presidents and friends around me ; and that the loss of some aged and venerable friends has not thinned our ranks, but that I am still supported bv the Nobles of our land. In their name I say, that much as many of them may and do feel the value of public support and opinion, there is no support and opinion to which they attach a higher value than to the approbation of this Meeting. We are here assembled in a noble cause : and feel that we are surrounded by those, on the sincerity of whose opinion, and the constancy of whose support, while we endeavour to deserve it, we can confidently rely.

It is most gratifying to have to record, at last, an alleviation of the intense drought with which this island was afflicted. On the evening and night of Tuesday some light showers fell. They wrerc followed on Wednesday by a copious rain, which cannot have furnished less than a six weeks supply of water to those individuals whose buildings are properly spouted, and whose cisterns are in repair. It would seem that the rain has been universal, hut it is not unlikely, that the fall of water was unequal on different portions of the surface oi the island. For the present, it is probable, that solicitude may he allayed in relation to that form of ill ; but if the rainy season lias now commenced, and if it should he a heavy one, what security is there against a recurrence of the scenes of woe of 1810, 1823, and 1835. Are the streets of the town cleaner than they were in the first or in the last of the years which have been named 1 Is there any really practical mode of either making them so, or, if made so, of keeping them so. Let any one look at the abominations in the pit on the windward side of the road between town and þÿGambles great house, or at a similar receptacles for filth at every exit of St. John, and then answer if those are symptoms of civilization or of barbarism. Four thousand people, or nearly so, are congregated upon one hundred and sixty acres of land without one single institution, as relating to the town itseit, to shew that it is the abode of British subjects. No hospital, no scavenger, no arrangement to secu e a supply of water, no market, no authority effectually to prevent encroachments on the streets, in fact no one thing which can engender that distinct feeling of a town, that creates a community of mind, and a oneness of purpose among its inhabitants. This is not the first time that the want of some municipal authority has been urged on the public notice, by this paper, nor shall it

be the last. If an intelligent person were asked to point out the peculiarity which most distinguishes a citizen of London from a villager of New Caledonia, the answer would undoubtedly he the power of combining with his fellows for public objects, that is possessed by the former and not by the latter þÿ or, in other woi ds, the cause and the effect of the high civilization which the one possesses, while the other is not only destitute of it, but of every desire to attain to it. þÿ These arc the two extremities of the scale, between them every possible shade of moral and social advancement exists ; but as either end is approached so do union and its fruits increase on the one hand, or individual reliance, weakness, poverty, and distress hear down ail stable happiness upon the other. þÿ Antigua llerald, May 27.

Since our lust publication the Island has been again favored by an All bounti ful Providence, with copious rains, which have been eagerly absorbed by the hitherto parched and thirsty soil. Our Island has assumed a beautiful mantle of rich verdure, giving promise of a goodly harvest, and forming a great contrast with the dry and burnt appearance of vegetation, a month or two past. The Hurricane season has commenced with high winds and squalls, which on Wednesday night and this morning were somewhat threatening in appearance, but which we hope will terminate in nothing more alarming, than a succession of good weather for the Island. We should be inclined to think from the violence of the gusts, that the tip end of the tail of a Hurricane experienced somewhere to Windward might have reached us on Wednesday night and this day.

A petition from the Merchants of Georgetown was read, praying the Court to direct that the Officers in the Colonial Receiver General's Office and in the Registrar's Office, should receive the notes of the Colonial Bank and of the British Guiana Bank, in lieu of specie. The petitioners expressed their high gratitude for the establishment of two institutions so convenient as the Banks, and stated that the notes of the Banks were now current in the Colony, and equal to cash ; but that much inconvenience would be felt if they were not received as cash at the respective public offices. Captain Warren said that the British Guiana Bank had no authority to issue paper. The Governor said that the Court of Policy could give no instructions, either one way or another : the Registrar was responsible to the Supreme Court for the money deposited in ms office ; the Receiver-General was also bound in heavy securities ; the Court of Policy, if it granted the prayer of the petition, would incur heavier responsibilities than it ought to incur. Mr. Macrae did not think that the Court of Policy could interfere. þÿ Captain Warren said that the Home Government, in chartering the Colonial Bank, had, by no means, intended to make the notes of that Bank a legal tender. The Governor said that no hank notes were a legal tender, except the notes issued by the Bank of Eneven these were so, only in consequence of an express enactment of the Legislatuie; the þÿKing permission s to a Bank to

issue notes, did not make the notes a legal tender. Mr. Rose was understood to suggest, that the officers mentioned in the petition should be directed to receive the notes until further orders. The Governorþÿ I hope þÿyou not ll break, hut if you break, what will become of your notes ? Mr. Macrae remarked that the notes of the Colonial Bank were payable at Barbados. The Governor, in answer to a remark made by Mr. Rose, said that doubloons and dollars were not now a legal tender ; the recent proclamation did not make them a legal tender : only, the public office would receive them ; in the present instance, the most prudent wav would be for the Court not to interfere. The petition was declared to be rejected.

MAY 31, 1837. THE RIGHT HON. LORD BEXLEY IN THE CHAIR. Rev. JONATHAN GROWTH þÿER. My Lord, I should most willingly have remained altogether silent on this occasion, notwithstanding the invitation with which 1 have been favoured, to take a part in your proceedings: for I have nothing of importance to add to the statements already made : and can have no claim on your attention, except on the ground of those principles, which are so well known to be involved in the great cause itself which we are now assembled to support. My Lord, it has been my great privilege, from a child to know those Holy Scriptures, which are able to make men wise to salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus: from my earliest years, 1 have been taught to reverence those Scriptures, as the only and sufficient rule, both of faith and practice. J can, therefore, give the right-hand of fellowship to anv man holding the same principles: 1 am willing to co-operate with him, to unite with him, or to follow him, if he prefer that, in any service, by means of which we may promote that circulation of the word of God which it is our object to secure : and while I draw water from the well of Salvation with that urn that seems to suit me best, I am not offended with nry brother, because he draws with an urn of a colour or pattern different from my own. 1 can forget, in the prosecution of the great object, those minor circumstances, which create subordinate distinctions: and can put them aside with a stanza, accommodated to this point, from the writings of a

modern Poet : þÿ « My glass may be purple, and yours may be blue ; Cut while Ibey are þÿfill from d the «ame bright bowl, The man who can quarrel for difference of hue Deserves not the comfort they hriug to the þÿsoul. Sorry should I be, if, among the changes of these velocious times þÿ to adopt the expression of a Noble Speaker who has just left the room þÿ this Institution should be swept away ; or if, at any future time, its character should be so modified and altered, as that it should no longer constitute a common ground, on which Christians of all Denominations may meet together, and combine in principle and operation ! 1 should regard either of these events, as one of the greatest calamities that could possibly occur to the Church or to the world ! I will only add, with respect to the allusion which was made in the Report to the Negroes in the West Indies, and to the estimation in which they hold those copies of the Scriptures which have been so liberally distributed among them, that there is an Individual of that Race in this Hall, and on this platform, who was once in the bonds of Slavery ; but who has been, of late years, a INI inistcr of Christ, highly honoured by the success which God has given him in preaching the Gospel to his fid low- Negroes : that individual will he allowed, I trust, to address a few words to this Meeting.
