My Lords, Ladies, and Gentlemen, 1 do most unfeignedly feel that there must bo a great appearance of presumption þÿ and I fear somewhat more than the appearance þÿ for those persons, whose time is necessarily much occupied by pursuits which, if not uncongenial to the great concerns of this celebration, are at all events very distinct and far removed from them, to come forward in the presence, and it may be to the exclusion, of many who are so far better entitled to that preference. It is as if the casual gleaners were to put in their claim with the labourers through the entire day, for the honour of the harvest The best practical proof, then, that I can give you of my sense of this intrusion, will be its shortness : for even had I more moments at my command at present, than, unfortunately for myself, I feel that I have, I should think it both most inappropriate for myself, and most disrespectful towards you, to let the crude off shoots of my scanty labour take up the time and attention which may be dedicated to those who have laboured long, and toiled much, your in service the veterans of your pulpits þÿ and platforms the Missionaries and messengers þÿ of your zeal, and, i am happy to be informed that I may add, the converts of your love. þÿ As this Resolution, however, has been put into my hand, I did not feel myself at liberty to decline the office and honour of moving it; because 1 did wish that my testimony, however humble, should not be wanting ; and be-

cause I felt, that, however diversified and engrossing any of our separate and distinct avo- j which I (and I speak on behalf of all my brecations may be, yet triffling, indeed, and tran sitory, and altogether subordinate they must appear and they must he, comparison in with that great Cause which has formed this Socie-

ing þÿ that Cause, of which the Bible is the instrument, and the world the theatre. I could not fail to hear with the most lively and grateful satisfaction the testimony borne by the Report which has been read to us this day, to the great progress and extension of this Society, and the incentives which are thus supplied to our increased perseverance, and more strengthened union : and I will only so far diviate from the profession 1 have already made to you, as to add, that while, in the espousal and maintenance of such a cause as that in which this Society embarks, no absence of visible results or of palpable success could justify our languor, indifference, or despondency ; still at the same time, it must add cheerfulness to our exertions, that the cause appears to be continually exhibiting the tokens of Almighty approbation, and the impress of Infinite Power; and that we may humbly hope that we are not only desiring, hut hastening, the time of that great consummation, when, beneath the advance of the same cause, every strong and every dark hold of ignorance will he stormed and will be enlightened, and every baleful fire of superstition, in the superior rays of Gospel light, will have grown pale, and will have expired.

Rev. Mn. FRAZER, from Antigua. þÿ My Lord, Ladies, and Gentlemen, I am sure that 1 need an apology much more than those Noblemen and Gentlemen who have thought fit to make apologies to-day. The consciousness that I am speaking before persons who have enjoyed the benefits of European education, and even before Noblemen and Gentlemen distinguished no less for their talent than for their rank and respectability, not a little

embarrasses me. But I have two things to sav, which 1 hope will he an apology for me, in consenting to stand forward in this manner. The one is, that I suppose the present honoured company, or the company that assembles annually at the celebration ol the Bible Society, do not often hear the sentiments of persons of my complexion ; and certainly, in an Institution designed for the benefit of all mankind, and which invites the co operation of all mankind, it does appear desirable, occasionally at least, to hear the sentiments of persons of every hue, and of every tribe, and of every nation. The other thing which 1 have to mention is, that the Bible Society has laid under obligations the Negro race, to which I am related; and it would he criminal for me not to express the grateful sense which 1, and many more, have entertained of those obligations. It is now so long since I first heard of the Bible Society, that the recollection of the day is almost indistinct. One circumstance, however, occurs to me, in reviewing the time past, which is so pleasing, that I must he allowed to mention it. The first announcement of the Bible Society which I heard was from a voluntary Society formed by some Persons of Colour, who associated themselves together to form an Auxiliary to promote its great object. From that time to the present, I have heard and read about the Bible Society, and its benefits to mankind ; and that respect and reverence which 1 first felt lor it has been continually on the advance. The veneration

thren who know any thing of the Bible Society) þÿ the veneration we have for that blessed Book þÿ considering it as God's best boon, which makes known the best gift of His love, ty, and which has called together this Meet- : Jesus Christ our Lord is transferred, in a þÿ great measure, and reflected on, the Bible Society itself. We have also been greatly delighted with the spirit of the Bible Society: it has seemed to us a liberal, generous, and Christian Society. The spirit in which we have been presented with that Book has been a spirit of Christian kindness : and when we have opened the Book, wc have not seen any discrepancy between the circumstances under which it was brought to us and the contents of the Book itself. We have been able .also, to trace many of the advantages of the Bible Society during the period of its operation. þÿ Other Societies have sprung up in consequence of it, or have been much improved by it ; and it hath seemed to us as if God had said to this Society, as was said to Moses respecting the Seventy. þÿ I will take of the Spirit which is on thee, and put it on þÿthem. We have considered the Missionary as a welcome Messenger þÿ a Messenger of the skies : but even he could not bring us more than his one Bible, had it not been for the kindness of the Bible Society We consider that our Schools, valuable as they are, would have been, through the perverseness of human nature, as likely injure as to benefit us, hut to for the Bible Society. We consider that it is

the Bible that must make all our other blessings hallowed, for they arc sanctified by the word of God and prayer ; and thus in proportion as we reverence the Bible, and the spirit of the Bible so wc esteem more and more the British and Foreign Bible Society. I am glad to avail myself of an opportunity of expressing the sense of the obligation which 1 and many others feel for this Society, The Bible Society has distributed the word of God among the Slaves, for many years past :

the l3i!)!o Society furnished our Schools with Uibles and Testaments: and at the period of the Emancipation, the Bible Society sent us above 100,000 copies of Testaments and Psalters for tiie ne w 1 y deli vered Slaves, \\ ith what shall I compare this kindness, as it apbenevolent eflbrts peared to us ? Shall I Ebed of bring the case of the melech, whose deeds are recorded in Scripture, to relieve the oppressed Jeremiah / Shall I compare it to the philanthropy which has set light-houses on the shores of your country, to warn the mariner in the night, when tossed by tempests, of his danger, and to prevent his being wrecked on the sands? All these comparisons but faintly illustrate the benevolence which is exhibited by this Society, in sending to us the Bible. This was, indeed, to the Negro Race, like waving a torch across the gloom which enveloped us: this was to draw out your souls tous hungry and famishing men : this was to disover the spring in the burning desert, and to erv to us, þÿ Crane, come, without distinction ! and come all þÿ! This was to make us triumph over our condition, and to make us exclaim, þÿ Would to God that all men were even as we are, except our þÿbonds! I am happy to say, that in Antigua the Bible Society is very popular ; and that it does not want for advocates of distinguished literary abilities, nor for subscribers from every rank and grade in the community I have known your Agent, Mr. Thompson þÿ and Mr. Wheeler, whom I saw a little before 1 left

Antigua. He did not continue long with us ; but we saw enough of him to wish his return. 1 cannot sit down, without again repeating my thanks to all those who have shown so much friendship to the Negro Race, in the West Indies. My Lord, the language of sincerity and feeling is plain : it is simple, as it is sincere. All 1 can say is, We thank you! we thank you ! But perhaps another day will come þÿ certainly it will come, þÿ when tiiat Gr<at One, who is alone the Fountain of all honour and praise, will be revealed, and when lie shall sit upon His throne of Judgment ; and then some Gentlemen who have befriended the Negro llace, and conveyed to them the blessings of this Society, will hear Hint say, These could not recompense you; but you shall be recompensed at the Resurrection of the Just. Inasmuch as ye did it to one of tiie least of these my brethren, ye did it unto þÿme.

The King of England was very seriously ill at that date with a complaint, something like water in the chest. The London Times of J une 15th says : þÿ þÿ As a friend and master, þÿ husband and father, as a man, and as the þÿ Sovereign of a free people, King William þÿ 4th, has excited in a powerful manner the þÿ sympathies of every honest Englishman, by þÿ the very serious nature of the malady, unþÿ der which, for some weeks past, he has been þÿ suffering. þÿ We fear we might with truth V say sinking ; for greatly it is to be apprehended that whatever changes may have occurred in the personal condition of Mis þÿ Majesty, they cannot be regarded as on the þÿ side ot convalescence. To speak frankly þÿ our feelings both of lively alarm and of deep þÿ and (with all deference) affectionate conþÿ ceru, we acknowledge ourselves to be hopeþÿ less of any but one þÿ and that the least cheerþÿ result, of the ing malady, or complication of maladies, which has of late oppressed the þÿ frame of the kind and good King William þÿ þÿ Nor, so far as human judgement can deterþÿ mine, do we understand that there exists the þÿ least rational ground for conjecturing that þÿ the event will be long postponed." The Lords have again postponed the consideration of the Irish Municipal bill from the 9th of June to the 3rd of July, on motion of Lord Lyndhurst. In the event of the demise of the King, a dissolution of parliament, and a new election

follow of course. Bulletins signed by three Physicians are daily issued of the state of His Majestvs health. In Spain Irrabaen succeeded in overtaking Don Carlos on the 24th May, not far from Huesca; a desperate battle ensued, w hich resulted in the defeat of the þÿQueen stroops, who retreated, leaving Irrabaen, Vicerov of Navarre, and commander in chief of the Queen's Army on the side of Victoria, dangerously wounded, and he is since dead The accounts from ISpain since that date are very confused. Another battle is said to have been fought on the 2d and 3d June, very bloody, in which the Carlists lost 2,000 killed, Don Sebastian and Villareal were both wounded ; it is said no quarter was given. Don Carlos ciossed the river Cinca on the 5th of June, þÿ the commander of the French foreign legion, General Conrad, was killed tin the above battle. The battle of the 2d June was fought near Barba3tro. þÿ Don Carlos was approaching Saragossa (in possession of the Queen) Cabrera was within ten leagues of that city, but he had not yet formed a junction with Don Carlos, who had entered Catalonia. Espartero advanced upon Tudela on the 7th June with lli battalions, (about 10,000 men) leaving the residue of his army in the environs of Hornani. þÿ General Evans has returned to England, and his legion has been paid þÿoff a part of it (about 1500) have reinlisted, under General þÿO Connell. þÿ It is said there is no force in front of Don Carlos, suf. lieiently strong to prevent his advance þÿ the in-

The Public notice from the Colonial Bank, which appears to-day, must be very gratifying j to all those who are favourably disposed to the I Institution, and must convince the few who have been sceptical in their opinions as to its capabilities, of the firm footing on which the Directors have commenced their important and highly useful operations. Many persons seem to have not read the Charter, or have forgotten the chief features of it, else they would have hazarded the expression of those idle and absurd predictions of the inability of the Company to carry on business with advantage to the public. It should be recollected that by the terms of the Charter, the Company were not allowed to commence their operations until the sum of five hundred thousand pounds sterling, one fourth of the capital, had been paid in. þÿ This important fact is announced by a public advertisement in the London Times, that great and influential Commercial Journal which circulates in every part of the world. The notice in the Times appears in our paper of this evening The prospect of the Colonial Bank spreading its beneficial effects throughout all the ramifications of Colonial society, is cheering in the extreme Though not conversant with insti- j on tutions of this kind, and having had little to j do with the intricacies of monetary concerns, we have from observing facts in the history of the Mother Country, been induced to entertain sanguine hopes of the usefulness of a Bank in this quarter of the British empire;

and we have no fear of disappointment in our expectations. The system of Cash credits, as their mode of advancing money is technically termed, we should think calculated to aflbrd great assistance to many individuals. A person, having occasion for a sum of money, say £500, oilers two sufficient securities, who give a Bond to the Bank for the repayment of the loan when required, lie has

j\T33. his Bill, or whatever authority may be given him for drawing the said moncy-He may require perhaps, only £100 of the money þÿ he receives it, out pays no interest until this money is in his hands þÿ and whatever sum he repays to the Bank, so much interest is stopped þÿ lie uses such portions of the loan as he requires, at his pleasure, and paying interest only on what he draws out. This is giving great facility to persons wanting occasionally sums of money, provided they can obtain friends to answer for their ultimately repaying the money when required at the Bank. The very general circulation of the Colonial Bank notes has been found very useful in our Island We trust that the more people know of this institution, the more generally its value will be appreciated.

We are now to notice another Joint Stock affair, but of a very different description. An Ice Company is now established in this town, a house built for the reception and keeping of this useful article, and a cargo actually now deposited within an arched wall of great thickness, on the Pier. The Building is not altogether completed, but we understand it will be a striking and handsome object. This Ice establishment is a cold concern to be sure ; yet it may be rendered a powerful agent for exciting warmth in the human body, from the very facility which it affords for cooling our drinks. It must be delightful in this climate to have our Punch, Sangaree, and Malt, cooled with Ice, and we hear much is daily sold for that luxurious enjoyment ; but, as u:e belong to a, not the Temperance Society, we would warn our friends to have a special care, lest in heir eager desire to quench their thirst with cool liquor, þÿ they þÿcontinue pouring in the delicious draft, þÿ till wine, or some other equally dangerous liquor þÿ inflame them" and that, which is sent as a blessing, be turned into a curse. With this little hit of moralizing, (our friends know it is an old and confirmed habit of ours), we conclude with our best wishes for the success of the Company ; and that the water, which can be thus wonderfully preserved in a congealed state in these regions of the Sun, may be made available for the health of our people. From the New York Herald, April 29. MONEY MARKET. Saturday, April 29. The gloom and despondancy increase a pace. Yesterday, stocks took another tumble þÿ almost every one on the list, except two or three, falling several per cent. United States is now down to 111 þÿ and the best bank stock in the street below par. Dry Dock and many others have fallen 50 percent from their highest quotations in two months Utica Rail Road is at par, and every other under par, more or less. Failures also continue, and when they are to stop, no one can predict. There is, however, a much heavier calamity impending over the money market that the failures of mercantile houses, or the expected bad news from England. U udcr the influence, and by the repeated advice of the government, the mass of the people are gradually abstracting the specie from the banks. This drain was first set in motion by the Ex-President, in his efforts to restore a specie currency, and if it goes on a lew months longer, there is not a bank in the nation that will not have to suspend specie payments. The only dependence of the bank is now on the depositors. If they were to take alarm, the whole fabric of paper credit would receive its final blow. From New Orleans we learn that the country people þÿ the great mass þÿ are continually changing their paper money for specie. The same spirit exists here. In a very few months, a single bank, the Dry Dock, has paid out an amount of specie equal to its capital ; and if we take that as a specimen, it may be asserted with safety, that all the banks of this

state have paid out an amount equal to twice their capitals during the last year. Our banks in the city have probably $2,500,000 in specie, and the United States Bank about the same sum. A short time since, an agent of a country bank presented to a government bank a check of Prime & Co., for $20,000 and demanded specie. It was to aid the country bank. The city bank refused, replying that they had entered into an arrangement with the drawer, not to pay any specie until the government made another draft upon them. It seems that some government draft had recently been refused to be paid in specie þÿ Other arrangements are in existence with other foreign exchange houses, not to draw specie, unless treasury drafts should be presen led for payment. But, while the gold and silver increases among the people, it decreases in a like ratio, in the vaults of the banks. This, therefore, is the alarming point of the present crisis. The government and the party taught the doctrine of gold and silver. The people have become believers and carry it out. The government banks joined in the new' crusade, merely foi the purpose of getting the use of the public deposits. In the present state of public opinion, the impulse will not cease and cannot be stopped. While the banks have extended their loans and circulation beyond all former precedent, the great mass of :h ; community are silently drawing from beneath them, the very prop that they stand þÿupon. England cries out for gold to sustain her sys-

tem, and complains that the United States h ive more of the specie basis than tliev want. The United þÿStates or rather our þÿbanks cannot comply with the demand, because they have not got it. Our own government is also a creditor to our banks for forty millions, but

This is our present condition, but we have yet to see the end. It is a struggle between the government, the depositors, and the community, which shall get the gold and silver. þÿ The latter will succeed and it is likely that both government and depositors will follow the fate of the merchants. AGE OF REVOLUTION. We are in the commencement of a series of revolutions þÿ philosophical, financial, commercial, social, political, literary, and religious There can be no mistake in the signs of the times. The original and wonderful movement of the human mind has began contemporaneously in the old and the new world The Anglo-Saxon race, transplanted into this he misphere, have begun a revolution that will not pause till the whole world shall be changed. It is a remarkable fact in the history of the human race that the germs of revolutions, and the original discoveries that lead to revolutions, always come before the world in clusters. In every age the lights of genius start up in groups. Luther, Galileo, Bacon, Shaks peare, Milton, Harrington, Newton, and all the parent minds that broke the spell of the middle ages, were parts of the same system þÿ separate lights forming the same group of mind, capable of creating a new world and giving the generations of man a new impulse. During the space of the two or three last centuries all branches of knowledge, science, art, and learning have made wonderful progress under the original impulse which was given by the mighty minds of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The steam þÿengine the system of commerce þÿ the art of war þÿ the science of government þÿ the purification of religion þÿ the advancement of society and manners, now prevailing in the world are the offspring of the same spirit which discovered the new world, shook the Romish tiara, and struck

out the new philosophy of Bacon and Newton. We are in the commencement of a new, fresh, and more exciting age than what we have just passed. The revolution now going on in the financial, commercial, social and political world, both in this country and in Europe, is only a wholesome preparation for the wonders that are almost ready to leap into existence. There cannot be the slightest doubt but the practical discovery made by the humble blacksmith of Vermont, will form the beginning ol a new era þÿ a new philosophy and a new order of civilization. The whole world is in a state of tumult þÿ but it is the tumult of genius þÿ the agitation of intellect þÿ the movement of the human mind in search of a higher order of civilization þÿ a higher species of existence. The discovery that lightening, electricity, galvanism, the principle of life, the power of gravitation are all identical þÿ all resolvable into one principle, and can be made to perform any work in any assignable operation in human life, is ushered upon the world at a time when a similar revolution in agitating the financial, social, commercial and political systems. On the works and fragments of the old system of life and business, the newly developed power will facilitate the creation of new systems more practical, more energetic, more useful, and more favorable to the higher order ol intelligence and civilization. What

a singular coincidence that the paper systems of commerce and currency should he falling into ruin by their own weight, at a moment when a new þÿpow er is coming into being that will sweep every steamboat and ship from our waters ; and by its energy, speed, velocity and safety make whole countries and continents as contiguous as the streets of a single city I The power of galvanism devoted to locomotion of all kinds cannot fail in twenty years to change the whole face of the civilized portion of the earth. There never was such a revolution in the world as that we are just entering þÿupon a revolution, radical, intellectual, financial, in every shape or form that mind can imagine. þÿ Let not our readers suppose for a moment that these sentiments and views are extravagant. They are the sober and deliberate convictions, resulting from a personal knowledge of the great principle brought to light by Mr. Davenport, coupled with a deep consideration of the events going on in the world around. þÿ The failures and distresses and agitations, political and commercial, are only the spring showers that precede the opening of a long and beautiful and radiant summer of science and civilization. Oh I that I were twenty years younger I or could come to file again in the year 1919, when all the world will he revolutionized, and vovages to Europe will he made in a week, and news transmitted to New Orleans, on the galvanic principle, in a couple of hours I

AI, MACKS. The rise of Almacks may serve to illustrate the mode in which this sort of empire was consolidated. A few pretty women, not in the highest rank of the nobility, met at Devonshire House to practice Quadrilles, then recently imported from the continent. The establishment of a subscription ball was suggested, to whieh none but the very elite were to be admissible; the subscription to be low, with the view of checking the obtrusive vulgarity of wealth. The fancy took, and when it transpired that the patroness had actually refused a most estimable English duchess, all London became mad to be admitted ; exclusion was universally regarded as a positive loss of caste, and no arts of solicitation were left untried to avert so horrible a catastrophe. The wives and daughters of the oldest provincial gentry, with pedigrees traced up to the Heptarchy, have been seen humbling themselves by the lowest acts of degradation to soften the obduracy of the autocratesses ; and we fear it is no exageration to say that more than one parvenu had been known to barter his vote in parliament, and more than one parvenu her honour, for a ball ticket. The prestige has gradually abated, and the institution is now tottering to its fall ; but its origin is worth recording, as a ludicrous phenomenon in the progress of society. þÿ Quarterly Review.

From the New York Gazette, April 29. A magnificent discovery. þÿ Mr. Thomas Davenport, a Vermont blacksmith, hut a most intelligent man, and one of those original and acute thinkers to whom our world is indebted for the most important improvements that

in motive power that really seems likely to supersede all other contrivances for þÿ getting along in the þÿworld þÿ whether in travelling on the land or voyaging on the þÿwater whether it be in making money by the propulsion of machinery in manufactures, or in the rapidity of our motion over rail roads. We of course speak with diffidence of matters with which we are not conversant, but we have the right we suppose, to form conclusions from the opinions of those who are conversant in a given matter, and it is principally upon the strength of those opinions, that we speak now. Mr. Davenport has discovered a mode of supplying Magnetic and Electro magnetic power, which we have good grounds for believing will be of immense importance to the world. He has machines now in this city, which go very far to warrant the most sanguine anticipations of a total revolution in mechanics. We have not seen them, because our other avocations have prevented it, but we have read Professor þÿSilliman description s of them, and we are convinced from that, that a new era is about to commence in these matters. We recommend to every reader a perusal of the þÿProfessor article s on this subject, jn the American Journal of Science and the Arts, for April, 1837. In the mean time, we copy the best account that we have seen of the practical operation of the machine in this city, from the New Era, whose editor is au fait in these things ; only adding that Mr. Edwin Williams is agent for the patentees,

and will give all required information on the subject. Who Mr. Williams is, will hardly be enquired of by those who know any thing about the Annual Register. 1. We saw a small cylindrical battery, about 9 inches in length, 3 or 4 in diameter, produce a magnetic power of about 300 lbs. and which therefore we could not move with our utmost strength. No. 2. We saw a small wheel five and a half inches in diameter, performing more than 600 revolutions in a minute, and lift a weight of 24 lbs one foot per minute, from the power of a battery of still smaller dimensions. 3. We saw a model of a locomotive engine, travelling on a circular rail road with immense velocity, and rapidly ascending an inclined plane of far greater elevation than hitherto ascended by steam power. And these and various other experiments which we saw, convinced us of the truth of the opinion expressed by Prof. Silliman, Renwf k, and others, that the power of machinery may be increased from this source beyond an assignable limits. It is computed by these learned men, that a circular galvanic battery, about 3 feet in diameter, with magnets of a proportionable surface, would produce at least an hundred horse power, and therefore that two such batteries would be sufficient to propel ships of the largest class across the Atlantic. The only materials required to generate and continue this power for such a voyage, W'ould be a few thin sheets of copper and zinc, and a few gallons of mineral water. Whilst the cost ol this new motive power

is merely nominal, it is perfectly safe and manageable. There is not a possibility of auy shock or explosion, and the whole machinery might be conducted by a child. We hastily announce these important features of this incalculably important invention, preparatory lc a more scientific and practical elucidation.

From the New York Gazette, April 29. Latest from Mexico þÿ By the arrival of the schr. Cumanchc from Matamoras, we have received our regular files of the Mereurio ; they contain nothing interesting from the interior. Private letters and verbal reports of passengers by the Oumanehe announce that the army at Matamoras was in the most deplorable condition, without provisions and clothing, and in the most complete destitution. General Bravo, fatigued by the eternal complaints and murmurs of the soldiery, has been obliged to resign and abandon the army. This confirms an article in the Mereurio, of which the following is a translation : þÿ Every day renders the position of the General commanding the army more difficult and painful. That virtuous citizen has suffered alike from the vain and frivolous promises of the government assistants, and trom the perfidy of the contractors. He is in absolute want of every thing : and yet, up to this time, he has courageously sustained this hard situation in the hope that sooner or later his difficulties would have an end. The 150,000 dollars which Quintaua promised should be sent him, have not arrived, and from all appearances never will. The provisions ordered at New Orleans, and for which 830,000 ought to have been remitted, have been expected in vain. In these circumstances public confidence is annihilated, and the commissary not having it in his power to collect a cent from any branch of revenue, can obtain no credit ; and thus Gen. Bravo, with 0000 men on his

hands, is left without the means of paying or feeding them. Such is the situation of the chief of the army ; such is the condition into which the government and its contractors have thrown us. As it is impossible to calculate the results of the painful situation, we have thought ourselves obliged to make it known in order that should any misfortune happen, the authors of it may not be concealþÿed. We learn also that all idea of the expedition against Texas is abandoned, and that the troops were on the point of being disbanded. In every other respect Matamoras was perfectly tranquil.

From the same paper of the 21st. MEXICO. Private letters from Mexico to the 28th ult. confirm the intelligence of the arrival at Vera Cruz of the French national brig of war La Badine, the frigate Didon of 64 guns, and two other brigs. These vessels arc under the command of Capt. Bretomere, and require in the name of France reparation and indemnity from the republic of Mexico. This claim cannot but prove highly embarrassing at this moment to our neighbour, and render her affairs still more complicated and critical. The events of the 1 1th March were passed almost unnoticed by us, for accustomed as we have been to the continual repitition of pronunciamentos and revolutions, we have regarded with the same vision all the events that transpire in that volcanic country. It appears, however, that a serious crisis is to date from the reduction of the copper coin 50 per cent "We shall let one of our correspondents give his views upon the subject, and then our read, ers will be competent to judge of the danger to which the general safety was exposed, es pccially the safety of foreigners.

þÿ þÿNever, says he, þÿ has a revolution exhibited itself under a more formidable aspect that this last. On the 10th of this month Mexico was threatened with a contest of the most frightful character. The whole population encumbered the squares and principal streets. All the stores were closed ; the doors barricaded, and each one with the most fatal coldness waited the signal for pillage. Horses, carriages, sellers, peaceable persons, all had disappeared to give room to a wild population vomited forth by the tauxbourgs þÿ! The government exhibited a great deal of vigor : in a moment the great square was covered with troops, who drove back the people from all quarters. Numerous patroles were placed in all directions, and the untortunate people, ignorant of their great loice were driven, chased away without obtaining the least satisfaction or justice. þÿ You cannot conceive to what a state of misery this beautiful city is reduced. i he government do not pay any tiling, no not even to the army which defends it. The soldier, the employer, the pensioned widow, are all dying with hunger ! The more the public distress augments, the higher is the pri«e of provisions ; and a sack of corn is sold for 815 which is more than three times its value. þÿ Another grievance not less dreadful, is the abuse of the copper coin. The republic is flooded w ith Cuariillas. It seems there are no more dollars, at least they have disappeared to so great an extent, that merchants lose 40 per cent upon the change in copper. It was

to remedy this evil that the sage and wise deputies in taking into consideration the public calamities, thought it alone necessary to change the value of the cuartillas, making them worth one half of their nominal value ; and this they did by the law of the 1 1th of March. By it the possessor is made to lose one half of his legitimate gains. And as the government has more than eight millions of cuartillas in circulation, the people are made the losers of four millions. These are the motives for a revolt which if it did not terminate fatally is to be attributed to the vigilance of the government and the fidelity of the troops. But the fire has alone been partially smothered to break out upon another occasion with still greater fury." Such is a faithful picture of a country which the bad faith of the governing power, the cupidity of the men in office and the fatal ambition of a few individuals, are conducting towards an impenetrable abyss ! Such is a true exhibit of the state of things at the moment when France, the United States and England are requiring indemnities and reparations ! And to the incapacity of the rulers, the insolence of a cabinet characterized by ignorance and embecillitv, are the demands of three great nations to be referred for adjustment ! Assuredly we should deplore the late of an unfortunate people, whose courage and sacrifices serve only to advence the military or political fortunes of a few ambitious and designing men !

From the Barbados Mercury, May 16, 1837. By the mail-boat Eleanor, we yesterday received a supply of colonial papers. The Grenada and Trinidad Journals, we are sorry to find, continue to publish statements of the increased number of cases of small pox in those islands, in the former of which it appears there are no le -s than 385 persons suffering from that loathsome and horrible disease. In Trinidad the Governor had found it necessary to enforce the quarantine law, with the utmost rigour, and his Excellency had also very humanely extended support and assistance to the sick. þÿ One or two shocking murders had been recently committed in Trinidad.

The departure of Colonel Sir C. F Smith from this island, to take the command of the Koval Engineers, at Gibraltar, has we fund, drawn from Sir S. Whittingham the following general order, expressive of the extent and value of the services of Sir Charles during a period of 14 years. It certainly must be a source of heartfelt satisfaction to Sir Charles, to find that his public conduct has been thus appreciated by an officer of such high standing in the army as Sir Samford Whittingham, and as Sir Charles is about to reap the reward of almost a whole life spent in the active and faithful discharge of his professional duties, in this and other quarters of the globe, it is to be hoped that the appointment will be sucli as to compensate him amply for past services : þÿ general order. < Head Quarters. Barbados, Mth April, 1837. þÿ Colonel Sir Charles Smith, C. 15., my immediate predecessor in the command ol his þÿMajesty s troops in the Wind waid and Leeward islands, &c., having been appointed Commanding Koyal Engineer at Gibraltar, I feel it a duty I owe to him and the service, to offer ibis tribute of thunks for the very able manner in which he conducted this command previous to my arrival. Sir Charles þÿSmith s ervices in almost every part of his þÿMajesty s dominions, are too well known and too justly appreciated, to need any enlogium on my part; but it may not be so generally known, that in the Peninsular war, his services were so distinguished as to obtain for him the brightest laurel of which a

British soldier can he ambitious þÿ the confidence and esteem of the Duke of Wellington. Sir Charles' long and intimate acquaintance with the West Indies, during a period of 14 þÿyears service, makes his approaching departure, in a public point of view, a loss which I deeply deplore ; whilst as a friend of 24 years standing, I cannot but grieve that our re-union should have been for so short a period. Sir Charles takes with him my best wishes for his healtli and happiness, and my fervent hope that he may yet have many opportunities of rendering his country that good service of which no man is more capable. (Signed) Samford Whittingham. þÿ IAeut.-General Commanding the Forces.
SEIZURE OF HIS þÿMAJESTY SSLOOP LEVERET, BY A PORTUGUESE FORT.

( From tilt) Madras Herald, Dec. 28.) On the 23d of October, the day after date of our latest cape papers, the Leveret arrived iu Simon's Bay from the Mozambique Channel, bringing the following extraordinary intelligence. It appears that about the middle of last year, Captain Banco, the port captain at Cape town, had obtained information, from some vessel which arrived in Table Bay, that a large corvette, mounting 20 guns, had been fitted out as a slaver at Havannah, and despatched for a cargo to Madagascar. J his account was immediately transmitted to Ad-

miral 'nmpbclt, who lost no time in directing the Pelorus to proceed to the Mozambique channel in search of her. Though some accounts of the corvette were communicated to the Pelorus at the different ports, she failed in falling in with her. The Leveret, a 10 gun brig, commanded by Captain Bosanquct, being in the Mozambique Channel in the earjv part of December last, heard that a large slaver had just arrived ou the coast, and on the 25th of that mouth discovered her lying at anchor in a small bay. The corvette (for there is but little doubt of her being the same vessel which the Pelorus was in search of the preceding year, and whii h had returned to the coast after a successful voyage), refusing to hold communication with the brig, an action commenced. So desperate was the resistance the slaver made, that the Leveret hauled o!F twice to repair damages, and at length after having one man killed, and five or six wounded, amongst whom was the master, succeeded in taking possession of her. The exact loss of the slaver, which mounted twenty guns« and carried 70 or 80 men, was not mentioned, but must have been considerable. A large quantity of dollars, intended for the purchase of slaves, was found, and removed to the Lc. veret, which proceeded to a Portuguese settlement near Mozambique, the name of which is forgotten. The governor of this place demanded that the slaver should be given tip, which being refused by Captaiu Bozanquet, a large battery, under which the Leveret lay>

suddenly opened upon her, and obliged her to haul down her colours, immediate possession was taken by the Portuguese both .of the Leveret and slaver, and the prize dollars removed to the fort There happened to he lying at this place a Portuguese frigate, to whose commander Captain Bosanquct appealed in vain, the other declaring he could not interfere. After hold'ng possession of the Leveret eight days, she was delivered lip, and Captain Bozanquet immediately returned to Simon's Bay. It may be easily imagined what impression this singularly outrageous conduct of the Portuguese governor has pioduced every where. The moment the Thalia arrived (and she was daily expected) Admiral Campbell intended to proceed to the Mozambique with all the squadron he could muster, and little doubt is entertained by those who know the decided character of the Admiral, that ample reprisals will be made for this unprecented insult on the English flag. FRANCE. The marriage of the Duke of Orleans with the Princess of Mecklenburg Schwerin is said to be definitely arranged. The Princess is 24 years of age, and niece of the Emperor of Russia The marriage has been brought about by Prussia, and has received the sanction of the Holy Alliance. Paris continues rife with plots and rumors of plots, and fresh arrests are made almost daily. The persecution of the press continues. From 20,000 to 30,000 workmen are out of employ at Lyons, and consequently in want of bread, and but a very few of them can find employment on the embankments The Mayor of Lyons has drawn a faithful picture of their condition, which calls for prompt assistance. The sum of 20,000 francs distributed among them, by the order of the Minister of the Interior, gives only 70 cents to each individual The melancholy accounts from St. Etienne tend to increase this calamitous state of things. We are assured that two deputations from the departments of Loire and the Rhone have pressed ministers to alleviate this distress by some legislative measure. þÿ Pennsylvania April 26.

Fifteen Lord Bishops have conspired to throw out, in the House of Peers, the Bill for the Abolition of Church Rates ; and from the speeches of lay Lords in that House, as well as from those of Sir Hubert Peel and Lord Stanley, there can be little doubt the advice of the Bishops will be followed. What will Ministers do in such a dilemma? A great many speculations are afloat as to their probable course. Some imagine they will resign þÿ others think they will force the King to dissolve Parliament þÿ some are sure that ministers will prorogue Parliament for a short time, and send up the Bill a second time to the Lords and then, if it is rejected, throw themselves upon the people for support while þÿ others affirm, that the moment the Bill is kicked out by the Lords, the ministers will be kicked out by the King. What momentous thing will happen among these aristocratic wiseacres, is beyond our ken ; all we know is, that the Church Rates are abolished! and all the aristocracy united þÿ every man, woman and child, both Whig and Tory þÿ could not longer enforce their payment. The rate-payers are roused to resistance thoroughly the battle on þÿ this point between Dissenters and the Church þÿrages and one half of the aristocracy have given up the contest. 1'he question is, therefore, practically decided. The Dissenters are not such simpletons as to yield after gaining so advantageous a position. We care not how much Parliamentary contest there may be about the abolition or enforcing of the ex-

action of the money-worshiping Church þÿ it will all do good, by damaging the aristocracy and their church. We repeat that, practically, the church rates are already abolished, and the Bishops " may go whine." þÿ Morning Chronicle, March 19.

ing Chronicle, March 19 In June, 1833, there arrived at Stevens burgh a labouring man, 35 years of age, who soon after engaged himself to take charge of the farm of Mr. Samuel James, of this village. He represented himself to be from Orange county, New York, by name of Alexander Jackson. After living with Mr. James until January, 1834, he purchased a farm about nine miles from this place and shortly afterwards offered his hand in marriage to a young woman who resided in Mr James's family, an adopted child of Mr. James in þÿ fact she went by the name of Sarah James, and no person in this vicinity knew, until recently, that she was a natural daughter of that Gentleman. þÿ Mr. James objected to the match, but Jackson represented himself as a relation of th ; president of the United States; and being a good looking, and withal an intelligent person. Miss James was pleased with him, and urged her father to consent to their marriage. In the May following they were married, and Mr. James gave Jackson a handsome farm, adjoining his own, as Sarah's portion on which Jackson built himself a house, and they lived very happily together. Since their marriage Mrs. J amcs has borne her husband two fine boys, the youngest being at present but two months' old But let us give the history of Jackson, as now discovered by his own confession, and by the appearance of a person in this community who has turned all his domestic joys into a cup of bitterness, and rendered his poor wife heartbroken ! In the first place, then, his name is not Alexander

Jackson (and for the present we shall suppress his real name ) During his boyhood, he became the father of a female child þÿ the mother being of le peetable parentage, and, as it now appears, a relative of our respected townsman, whom Jackson has hitherto called fatl>er-iuþÿ law He soon left the scene of his disgrace, which is in Orange county, New York, and afterwards, for many years lived in tlto vicinity of Albany, where the individual who now exposed him, knew him by his real name. name was also well known to Mr James, as the father of his adopted daughter. þÿ Judge, then of the agony of all parties when it became known that the beautiful Sarah James was not a natural daughter of Mr. James, and that she discovered in her husband her own father I Truth is, indeed, stranger than fiction, for this is but a simple narrative of tacts. Morrison's fills. At the York Assizes on Wednesday T. la Mott of Hull, was indicted for having caused the man slaughter of Mary Rebecca Russell, bv administering Morrison's pills. Deceased never had good health long together, and had been in the habit of taking the pills for the last two years, but never more than from four to six. Getting however, worse, her husband applied to the prisoner, who ordered four of No. 1 to search out the disorder, and six the following morning to work it off; these were afterwards increased by the prisoner's direction to six and eight, and then ten and ten, and continued increasing them to 15 every three hours, till she died. At the inquest held on the body, it was proved that she died from inflammation of the stomach and intestines, and several Medical Gentlemen was of opinion that the composition of the pills þÿ gamboge, coloeynth, and Aloes þÿ would produce such inflammation. þÿ A host of witnesses were called to show that they had received great benefit from taking pills in great quantities, and the to prove the efficacy in almost every disease incident to the human frame þÿ Mr. Justice Patteson summed up at considerable length, and left it to the Jury to say whether tliey were satisfied that the pills administered by the prisoner had produced the inflammation which had caused death, and that he had so administered them without being qualified so to do þÿ The Jury, in about half an hour brought in a verdict, finding the prisoner guilty of manslaughter accompanied with a re-
commendation to mercy ; and the court sentenced him to nine months imprisonment.

( From the Nevis Post, April 2G, 1837') This being the day appointed to be observed as a day of solemn fast and humiliation in consequence of the late awful visitation of the night of the 18th inst an eloquent and impressive Sermon was preached in St. Paul's Church by the Rural Dean, the Hon and Reverend D. G. Davis from the lamentations ' of Jeremiah, 3rd Chapter, and 22d verse, þÿ It is of the Lord's mercies that ice are not consumed, because his compassions fail not." The Reverend Gentleman drew an affecting picture of the circumstances under which the inspired Prophet wrote, and in comparing them with those of the sufferers on the present occasion, set before his hearers in glowing colours the abundant Mercy of the Almighty in having preserved so many from personal danger in the midst of the havoc and destruction created by the devouring flames, and earnestly exhorted them to improve the present opportunity by self examination, and so to prove their own hearts, that the fiery trials, to which they had been exposed might ultimately lead to their benefit. In the afternoon an appropriate discourse was preached by the Rev. Mr. Musson Rector of St. Paul's from the 103d Psalm, and 10th verse. þÿ " He hath not dealt with us after our sins, nor rewarded us according to our iniquities." After expatiating upon the infinite mercv shown by the Almighty to sinful man through all ages of the world, and the abduracv and rebellion manifested notwithstanding such repeated mercies, he reminded his hearers of the forbearance of God in the late awful dis-
pensation, and exhorted them to show their gratitude for his goodness by forsaking all unholy ways, and cleaving unto the Lord their God.

Wa regret exceedingly to learn by New York advices of the 25th April, that the crisis in the money market, was by no means over þÿ 215 jailures had occurred in that city in one month, and to the enormous amount of sixty millions of Dollars ! in New Orleans it is slated the failures amount to Forty millions more ! and the New Orleans Banks are supposed to have lost all their capital þÿ great apprehensions are entertained of the effect these heavy failures will cause in England, after they are known there þÿ the Backets from thence are bringing back protested bills to a large amount þÿ the arnourd of acceptances under which six or seven leading American houses in England had placed themselves, was at one time Twenty millions Sterling ! at the last dates this amount was reduced to Twelve millions Sterling aided greatly by the assistance of the Bank of England þÿ in New York, thousands of laborers are thrown out of employ þÿ confidence destroyed, goods are sacrificed at is low prices, and every thing at a stand.

From the New York Herald, April 18. The Age op Revolutions. þÿ We are in the commencement of a great political revolution that will sweep over half the civilized world. England, France and the United States are just entering upon a new era. The great commercial revulsion, careering over these three countriesþÿ for it is felt in France as much as here þÿ is only the forerunner of a complete political change that may sweep the present possessors of power from their high places before another year shall have elapsed. Modern society is founded on mutable principles. Every ten or fifteen years a prodigious change is generated in men, classes, opinions, thoughts and feelings. The great reform in England by which the tory party were driven from power, was preceded by the commercial revolution of 1825. The crisis which drove Charles the X. from the throne of the Bourbons, and placed Louis Phillipe where he is, was the natural eliect of the same cause. The revolution in the commercial systems of modern nations generate all the great changes in political opinion. Take for example this city. If the commercial crisis had not broken out as it did. would the government party have sustained the defeat that they now have done ? No such thing. The terrible revolution in commerce produced an equally terrible revolution in men's thoughts So it will do in England þÿ so in France. If the American government grasps its hands on the specie now in this country, & prevents it from flowing back to England, a revolution will be caused

in that country in less than a year. Should the Bank of England suspend specie payments for the want of gold, the whole country would be inflamed with revolution at once. The present party in power in England are hostile to that institution. The joint-stock banks are their þÿpets but when these pets go to the tomb of tie Capulets. then will the party soon follow. We are on the eve of great events. The seed of revolution is sown in the three most civilized countries of the globe þÿ England, France and the United States. Let us prepare for extraordinary tilings. A revolution in England may for a day or two, restore the tory party to power, but it tends to strengthen the republican party for the onset. A like event in France, has the same tendency. In the United States expectation is exactly tl'C reverse. Here, we have been so badly governed, that a political revolution may make us better þÿ not worse.
